title: 'What Do You Need?' Wednesday: Works in Progress
author: Episcopal Academy CTL
summary: This weekly teacher newsletter from the Episcopal Academy Center for Teaching and Learning curates three items and a closer with its own commentary and a 'Try This' action for each. It begins with a Yale study in which teachers primed with a happy memory graded the same essay more generously than those primed with an unhappy one, and recommends checking your mood before grading or hiding student names. It then summarizes Tim Dasey's caution that popular claims about paper versus screen reading are narrower than headlines suggest, and advises asking whether a study measured immediate or delayed outcomes. Third, it draws on an Edutopia piece by Youki Terada to ask teachers 'What are you working on?' as a narrow, deliberate practice goal ahead of a PD day. The last word is Mike Tomlin's decade-long Minecraft city as an example of curiosity and detachment.
points: Teachers' own emotional state can shift grading without their noticing, so a thirty-second mood check or anonymized grading adds protection.
Research claims reach teachers secondhand and confirm what they already believe, so it helps to ask what a study actually measured and when.
Good teachers keep growing by choosing one specific part of their craft to work on deliberately, the way elite athletes and musicians do.
A narrow practice goal such as the questions asked during discussion is more useful than a vague term like engagement.
Cross-divisional conversations about craft are valuable because teachers at different grade levels often work on more similar problems than they realize.
quotes: Researchers asked 56 middle school teachers to spend five minutes writing about either a happy memory or an unhappy memory. Then these teachers graded one seventh grader’s narrative essay. The happy group rated the essay higher on overall quality, creativity, and spelling and punctuation.
We teachers are great at checking on student well-being, but we’re not always as great at checking on our own—and that trickle down effect can have real impacts on student learning and performance.

Before your next grading session or batch of comments, take thirty seconds to name how you're actually feeling. If the answer is somewhere around "not great," consider waiting a bit, or going back and re-assessing that batch of work.
His main point is about how teachers arrive at research. And that arrival is usually secondhand and confirmatory to what we already believe.
Whether you teach kindergarten or AP Chemistry, the question of what a study actually measured matters as much as what it found.
Instead, we’re wondering about what specific part of your craft you’re actively thinking about right now.

An answer like, “the kind of questions I ask during discussion to elicit all students’ thinking” is better than a cover term like “engagement.” And when you have your answer, don’t be afraid to ask a colleague what they’re working on. Great things happen when teachers talk about teaching.
